analysis.one_liner: Caps steel imports for five years and funds steelworker retiree health care with a tax on steel.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced in May 2001 and never received any committee or floor action before the 107th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rolled steel imports back to average levels from the years before July 1997 using quotas or tariffs, created a federal trust fund that pays 75% of retiree health costs for steelworkers, and financed that fund with a new excise tax of up to 1.5% on steel sales. It would also have expanded a federal loan guarantee program for steel companies to $10 billion with 95% coverage, and offered up to $500 million in grants to merged steel companies to cover their environmental compliance costs, as long as the mergers kept at least 80% of steel jobs and facilities. The bill never got past its committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Domestic steel and iron ore producers, whose market share would have been protected by the import caps and who would have received larger federal loan guarantees and merger grants; steelworkers, whose jobs and plants would have been retained through the consolidation conditions; and steelworker retirees, whose health benefits would have been shored up by the trust fund.

how_it_helps.text: The bill directs the President to impose quotas, tariff surcharges, or negotiated export restraint agreements so that monthly steel imports stay at or below average pre-July 1997 levels, for five years.

It creates a Steelworker Retiree Health Care Trust Fund that pays 75% of qualified retiree health costs for eligible steelworkers and their beneficiaries, financed by an excise tax of up to 1.5% of the price of steel sold by manufacturers, producers, or importers.

It raises the Emergency Steel Loan Guarantee program from $1 billion to $10 billion in guaranteed loans outstanding, raises the maximum guarantee to 95% of principal and interest, and extends the program to 2015.

It authorizes $500 million in grants (up to $100 million per company) to merged steel companies to cover environmental compliance costs, available only if the merger retains at least 80% of steelworkers and 80% of steel-producing facilities, with clawback penalties if jobs or capacity fall below that level.

analysis.who_pays: Steel-buying manufacturers and consumers, who would face higher steel prices from the import caps plus the new excise tax on steel sales; and taxpayers, who would stand behind up to $10 billion in 95%-guaranteed steel company loans.

drawbacks.text: Import caps and the excise tax would raise the price of steel for every American manufacturer and consumer that uses it, from car makers to construction firms, since the tax is levied on steel sales and quotas restrict supply.

The federal government would guarantee 95% of up to $10 billion in steel company loans, shifting the risk of steel company defaults from lenders to taxpayers, and would directly pay steel companies' environmental compliance bills through merger grants of up to $100 million each.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivered real help to one group of workers and retirees: steel communities hit by mill closings and lost retiree health coverage. But the way it paid for that help was to raise steel prices economy-wide and to socialize steel company debt risk through loan guarantees and compliance grants. It protected an industry and its workforce together, and the broad cost of higher steel prices fell on everyone else.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced; the committee never acted on it, and the bill died when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced by Senator Wellstone on May 24, 2001, with seven cosponsors, and was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance that same day.
No further action was ever recorded: the bill received no committee markup, no floor vote, and never reached the Senate calendar before the Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Steel-consuming manufacturers and their customers, who avoided the higher steel prices the import caps and excise tax would have produced, along with foreign steel exporters who kept full access to the U.S. market. Steelworker retirees and distressed steel companies did not get the rescue the bill offered.

for.name: Sen. Paul Wellstone
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on it.

for.name: 7 senators (6 of 49 Senate Democrats, 1 of 49 Senate Republicans)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; the Senate record shows 6 Democratic and 1 Republican cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral in May 2001 and never took any recorded action on it, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Sen. Max Baucus
against.what_they_did: Chaired the Finance Committee during the period the bill sat there; no committee consideration of the bill ever occurred.

against.name: Steel-consuming manufacturers
against.role: U.S. industries that buy steel (autos, machinery, construction)
against.what_they_did: Opposed steel import quota legislation as a coalition during this period, arguing it would raise their input costs.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and six of the seven cosponsors were Democrats; one Republican joined. No vote ever occurred, so the broader partisan split was never tested.

industries.industry: Domestic steel and iron ore producers
industries.note: The bill would hand them protected market share through import caps, $10 billion in 95%-guaranteed federal loans, and grants covering their environmental compliance costs. Those gains come directly out of higher prices paid by steel users.

The import caps and job-retention conditions on mergers protect steel jobs, and the trust fund would pay 75% of retiree health costs for steelworkers who lost or risked losing coverage when mills closed.
Quotas restrict their steel supply and the excise tax adds up to 1.5% to the price of every ton of steel sold; these costs would ultimately be passed to consumers.
The bill expands federal guarantees to 95% of up to $10 billion in steel company loans, removing most of the default risk from lenders and placing it with taxpayers.
Import quotas and monitoring certificates would cut their access to the U.S. market back to pre-1997 levels; their cheaper steel had been holding prices down for American buyers.
